1	=================== heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect.md
2	# Correlation Can Hide a "Tie-In" Exercise That Is Actually Doing the Work
3	**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
4	analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
5	interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
6	5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
7	reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives a
8	single illustrative case (his own words: "we will illustrate with one example"): a training
9	session using three exercises, A, B, and C in sequence. After an experiment, results
10	improved in A and C but not in B. A high correlation between A and B suggested (wrongly)
11	that B was ineffective or non-transferring. A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained
12	only A and C — and this time **neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation:
13	exercise B had a "tie-in effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even
14	though B itself showed no measurable within-exercise result and its own pairwise
15	correlation to A/C looked unremarkable. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)
16	**Why it works** — No mechanism is proposed beyond the observation itself; Bondarchuk
17	explicitly defers this to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." The
18	described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
19	blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
20	pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
21	between two *other* exercises.
22	**When to apply** — Use as a standing caution whenever a program change removes an
23	exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
24	result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory
25	of other exercises in the same session/block before concluding it added nothing. This is
26	a genuinely underused idea in practical programming, where "cut what isn't working" is a
27	common simplification heuristic that this example directly complicates.
28	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This entire finding rests on a single
29	worked example ("we will address only one of the situations") with no stated sample size,
30	no statistical test, and no independent replication in the excerpted text — it is
31	presented by the author himself as an open question for future research, not a settled
32	result. Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise combination has a tie-in
33	effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what pairwise correlation studies
34	(including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect. Population and exercises A/B/C
35	are unspecified in the text (not named events or lifts), so there is nothing concrete to
36	generalize from besides the logical structure of the example.
37	**Example** — **Inference:** a strength coach who drops an unweighted plyometric drill
38	from a sprint-training session because the drill's own jump-height numbers aren't
39	improving might, per this heuristic, want to check whether removing it also flattens the
40	sprint-speed gains the program was otherwise seeing — the drill could be a tie-in exercise
41	even though its own metric looks stagnant.
42	**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific correlation blind spot;
43	flag for cross-reference if a future ingest (e.g., a sports-statistics or research-methods
44	source) covers interaction effects or mediation more formally.
45	confidence: untested
46	=================== heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle.md
47	# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle
48	**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
49	take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
50	though some individuals take 4-8 months. A general-preparation stage/block can only
51	function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the following specialized stage if it lasts
52	at least as long as that individual's own sports-form development timeline. He gives a
53	worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
54	15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
55	entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
56	needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
57	general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
58	(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
59	their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
60	endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
61	stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
62	transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
63	of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
64	(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
65	23-25.)
66	**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
67	entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
68	duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
69	that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
70	training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
71	developmental phase in itself.
72	**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
73	"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
74	phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
75	in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
76	it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
77	retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
78	days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
79	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
80	distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
81	developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.
82	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month (up to 4-8 month)
83	sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
84	specific citation in the excerpted pages, and is drawn from elite Soviet track and field
85	athletes on year-round training cycles. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
86	calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
87	sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
88	a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
89	adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
90	is more portable than the specific duration numbers.
91	**Example** — A 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very unlikely to
92	produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the Bondarchuk sense; it
93	functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training stress, and should
94	be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building a real strength or
95	conditioning "base."
96	**Related** — [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]] — the transfer-timing
97	model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
98	(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
99	duration question applies to.
100	confidence: supported
101	=================== heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling.md
102	# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration
103	**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
104	preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
105	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
106	[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
107	improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
108	conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
109	specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
110	necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
111	well as for carrying out restorative measures." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He goes
112	further, speculating that specialized-preparatory exercises may function as
113	"'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the transfer to
114	the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves — a direct
115	echo of the "tie-in effect" idea from Chapter 1 (see
116	[[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]). (PDF p. 175, printed
117	p. 158.)
118	**Why it works** — No new mechanism beyond the tie-in-effect hypothesis already flagged as
119	untested in Chapter 1; this is the author's own explicit hedge against a naive
120	misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data shows no further correlation,
121	therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns against).
122	**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
123	any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
124	athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
125	keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance (residual strength
126	retention, consistent with the roughly-30-day residual training effect windows this
127	library already tracks — see `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power") and for its
128	restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.
129	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
130	practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
131	separately tested finding in its own right — he flags his "stimulational factor" idea as
132	speculative ("it is very possible that... other methods... will be proposed"). Population
133	context is the same elite Soviet track and field throwers/sprinters/jumpers as the ceiling-
134	effect claims it responds to. Applying "keep it for maintenance, not for further gains" to
135	a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
136	directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
137	volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
138	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
139	training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
140	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
141	the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
142	different reasoning.
143	**Example** — A discus thrower whose squat numbers have plateaued relative to further
144	distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
145	and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
146	weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
147	than dropping squats from the program entirely.
148	**Related** — [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]] and
149	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the data findings this heuristic is
150	a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —
151	the Chapter 1 idea (tie-in effect) this heuristic's "stimulational factor" speculation
152	echoes.
153	confidence: supported
154	=================== claim--aerobic-anaerobic-energy-system-transfer-asymmetry.md
155	# Aerobic-to-Anaerobic-Alactate Transfer Is Broad and One-Directional; Anaerobic-Alactate-to-Aerobic Transfer Is Almost Absent
156	**What it is** — Tables 104-109 (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 149-154) report, for pairs
157	of energy-system training loads (aerobic, anaerobic-alactate, anaerobic-lactate), how many
158	of a set of physiological indices (heart rate, respiratory rate, lung ventilation, oxygen
159	reserve/debt, VO2max, blood lactate, energy expenditure/source, muscle fiber type, and
160	effect on time-to-sports-form) are "fully transferred," "frequently transferred," or
161	"non-transferred" from one training-load type to the other. The pattern is asymmetric, not
162	mutual, between each pair:
163	- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: mostly transferable — Bondarchuk states "6 of 7" of
164	  the cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices are "fully transferable" (Table 104,
165	  PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable factors are specifically blood-lactate
166	  level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with different
167	  fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers in
168	  anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
169	- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: broadly transferable both ways — "of the 16 tests
170	  looked at, only four were non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146); the
171	  anaerobic-lactate load actually *shortens* the time to enter sports form in aerobic
172	  training, while aerobic training does not shorten anaerobic-lactate's timeline (PDF pp.
173	  163-165, 171, printed pp. 146-148, 154).
174	- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: almost no transfer — "non-transferable factors here
175	  are all the remaining factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147),
176	  attributed to the oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus
177	  the oxygen-dependent structure of aerobic work.
178	- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: also limited, though the reverse direction
179	  (anaerobic-lactate loads shorten anaerobic-alactate's time to sports form, but not vice
180	  versa) shows a similar one-way asymmetry to the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate pair (Tables
181	  106-107, PDF pp. 164, 169, printed pp. 147, 152).
182	Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of the practical upshot of well-combined
183	aerobic/anaerobic training: "S. Auita" (almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held
184	world records simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within
185	tenths of a second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional
186	career bests: 200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11.
187	(PDF p. 172, printed p. 155.)
188	**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation is fiber-type recruitment: aerobic
189	training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers, while anaerobic-alactate and
190	anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch) fibers, and he states plainly
191	for at least one asymmetry that "it is not known why" one direction shortens
192	time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed p. 147) — the author
193	himself flags this as an open question, not a resolved mechanism. Do not read a fuller
194	physiological explanation into this than the fiber-type note the text actually gives.
195	**When to apply** — Use this asymmetry as a caution against assuming energy-system
196	training transfers symmetrically: a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for
197	anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate capacity (per the "fully transferred" majority in
198	Tables 104-105), but a block of anaerobic-alactate (pure sprint/power) work should **not**
199	be expected to build aerobic capacity — per this data it does not, on all but 2 of 15
200	tracked physiological indices. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all
201	three energy systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target
202	the intended adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning
203	and energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`) — this
204	entry's asymmetry finding sharpens that general principle into a specific, one-directional
205	claim about which energy-system work can substitute for which.
206	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported** for the aggregate Tables 104-109
207	findings (described as "collective data" in each table's own title, i.e. pooled across
208	Bondarchuk's tested athletes, sample size not stated in the excerpted pages).
209	**Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a single named-athlete case
210	offered as illustration, not independent evidence. The tested population is elite Soviet
211	and international middle/long-distance track athletes; the specific physiological index
212	values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
213	be treated as current normative standards. Applying this energy-system transfer asymmetry
214	directly to football conditioning (a repeated-sprint, intermittent-effort sport rather than
215	a continuous single-energy-system event) is Inference — no football or team-sport
216	population appears anywhere in this book.
217	**Example** — A program that substitutes heavy sprint/power ("anaerobic-alactate")
218	conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build aerobic capacity, is not
219	supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices showed no transfer in that
220	direction. The reverse substitution (using aerobic work to partially support
221	anaerobic-alactate capacity) has much more support in this data (Table 104).
222	**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer
223	asymmetry; cross-reference with `method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
224	for Eric's own energy-system programming framework, and with
225	[[claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]] for the companion finding
226	on how far training segment distances (rather than energy-system type) transfer within a
227	single distance-running event.
228	confidence: supported
229	=================== claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance.md
230	# The Longer the Competitive Distance, the Wider the Range of Segment Distances That Transfer to It — Except at the Ultra-Endurance Extreme
231	**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
232	segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
233	marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase
234	in the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments" — 800m
235	and 1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
236	steeplechase and women's 3000m start from 600m and 400m respectively; 5000m runners' range
237	starts around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women) — i.e., the
238	*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
239	longer. (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144.) Representative correlation values: men's
240	800m showed its strongest correlations with the 400m, 600m, and 1000m segments (0.700-0.912,
241	Table 89), with a sharp drop by the 1500m and further by 3000-5000m; women's 3000m showed
242	positive transfer across every tested segment, strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m
243	(0.725-0.906, Table 99). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners
244	(and 10km-walk women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer*
245	than the competitive distance, "because in sports practice similar tests do not exist" —
246	there is nothing longer to test against. (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
247	running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
248	(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
249	(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)
250	**Why it works** — Bondarchuk attributes the general pattern to "the specifics of the
251	interaction of systems involved in the training effect" — different aerobic/anaerobic-
252	alactate/anaerobic-lactate energy-system demands at different distances (general systemic
253	reactions) plus the individual athlete's short- and long-term adaptational responses
254	(specific reactions). (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) He does not fully resolve *why* the
255	transfer range widens with distance beyond this general systems-interaction language.
256	**Inference:** one possible reading is that longer events draw on a broader mix of energy
257	systems and pacing demands, so a wider band of training distances can stress a
258	physiologically relevant system for that event; this interpretation is this entry's own
259	reading, not stated by the author, and no outside exercise-physiology source was checked
260	in this ingest to confirm it.
261	**When to apply** — Use as historical support for distance-specific training range
262	selection: shorter competitive events (800m-1500m) can be trained effectively with a
263	narrower, shorter set of segment distances; longer events (5000m-marathon) benefit from
264	(and require) a wider spread of training distances, from well below race distance up to
265	race distance itself, to cover the full transfer range this data shows. **Eric's
266	baseline:** HHPR 5355 already treats aerobic-system training for speed-power athletes as
267	mainly serving inter-effort recovery rather than distance capacity, kept below anaerobic
268	threshold at roughly a 1:1-1:2 work:rest ratio (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and
269	energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.51`) — this book's population is exclusively
270	dedicated distance-event specialists, a very different training context from a
271	speed-power athlete's incidental aerobic work, so this entry's distance-range findings
272	should not be imported into football conditioning design without that distinction in mind.
273	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
274	middle/long/ultra-distance runners and race walkers, both sexes; the specific segment
275	distances and correlation values are dataset-specific. This entry covers **running/walking
276	segment distances only** — it says nothing about strength, jump, or throw-exercise
277	transfer to endurance events (not tested in this chapter). Applying "wider transfer range
278	for longer events" to a team-sport repeated-sprint or intermittent-endurance context
279	(football's actual endurance demand, per `method-baseline.md`'s energy-systems framing) is
280	Inference: football conditioning is not a single continuous-distance competitive event in
281	the way every sport in this dataset is.
282	**Example** — A 10,000m runner's program using training distances from 600m intervals up
283	to marathon-length long runs is well-supported by this data's transfer-range findings; a
284	marathoner's program should not expect any additional transfer benefit from segments
285	longer than the marathon itself, since no such segment exists to test or train.
286	**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — general classification
287	these segment distances fall under (specialized-developmental to competitive, depending on
288	how close the segment is to full race distance).
289	confidence: supported
290	=================== claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns.md
291	# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier
292	**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
293	jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
294	vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
295	running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
296	exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
297	consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
298	jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
299	women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
300	0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
301	for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). **High
302	jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
303	"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
304	0.400 level" for running exercises specifically. Instead, per his prose (PDF p. 105,
305	printed p. 88), "the most informative and transferable exercise appears to be the vertical
306	jump with a short run-up," at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women) — **note an
307	unresolved source discrepancy**: those exact figures match the "10-fold jump from place"
308	row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965), not the row literally labeled
309	"Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women 0.680-0.808, which
310	the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may be a
311	translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's row
312	label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian or
313	a second translation. Barbell snatch showed almost no
314	transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
315	with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
316	levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)
317	**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
318	**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
319	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
320	event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
321	the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
322	closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
323	general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested, but this
324	connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation. High
325	jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
326	explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
327	takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
328	straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
329	"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.
330	**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
331	supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
332	highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
333	with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
334	vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.
335	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
336	long jumpers, high jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole vaulters, both sexes. The "high jump
337	breaks the pattern" finding is specific to Bondarchuk's Soviet-era high jump technique
338	population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
339	should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
340	stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
341	football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
342	data exists in this source.
343	**Example** — A long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique jumps (at
344	reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
345	well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
346	short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
347	transfers the same way.
348	**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
349	explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
350	[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
351	sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).
352	confidence: supported

=================== heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect.md
# Correlation Can Hide a "Tie-In" Exercise That Is Actually Doing the Work
**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives a
single illustrative case (his own words: "we will illustrate with one example"): a training
session using three exercises, A, B, and C in sequence. After an experiment, results
improved in A and C but not in B. A high correlation between A and B suggested (wrongly)
that B was ineffective or non-transferring. A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained
only A and C — and this time **neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation:
exercise B had a "tie-in effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even
though B itself showed no measurable within-exercise result and its own pairwise
correlation to A/C looked unremarkable. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)
**Why it works** — No mechanism is proposed beyond the observation itself; Bondarchuk
explicitly defers this to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." The
described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
between two *other* exercises.
**When to apply** — Use as a standing caution whenever a program change removes an
exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory
of other exercises in the same session/block before concluding it added nothing. This is
a genuinely underused idea in practical programming, where "cut what isn't working" is a
common simplification heuristic that this example directly complicates.

result. Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise combination has a tie-in
effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what pairwise correlation studies
(including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect. Population and exercises A/B/C
are unspecified in the text (not named events or lifts), so there is nothing concrete to
generalize from besides the logical structure of the example.

from a sprint-training session because the drill's own jump-height numbers aren't

even though its own metric looks stagnant.

=================== heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle.md
# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle
**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
though some individuals take 4-8 months. A general-preparation stage/block can only
function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the following specialized stage if it lasts
at least as long as that individual's own sports-form development timeline. He gives a
worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
23-25.)
**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
developmental phase in itself.
**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month (up to 4-8 month)
sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
specific citation in the excerpted pages, and is drawn from elite Soviet track and field
athletes on year-round training cycles. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
is more portable than the specific duration numbers.
**Example** — A 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very unlikely to
produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the Bondarchuk sense; it
functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training stress, and should
be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building a real strength or
conditioning "base."
**Related** — [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]] — the transfer-timing
model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
duration question applies to.

=================== heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling.md
# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration
**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
well as for carrying out restorative measures." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He goes
further, speculating that specialized-preparatory exercises may function as
"'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the transfer to
the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves — a direct
echo of the "tie-in effect" idea from Chapter 1 (see
[[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]). (PDF p. 175, printed
p. 158.)
**Why it works** — No new mechanism beyond the tie-in-effect hypothesis already flagged as
untested in Chapter 1; this is the author's own explicit hedge against a naive
misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data shows no further correlation,
therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns against).
**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance (residual strength
retention, consistent with the roughly-30-day residual training effect windows this
library already tracks — see `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power") and for its
restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
separately tested finding in its own right — he flags his "stimulational factor" idea as
speculative ("it is very possible that... other methods... will be proposed"). Population
context is the same elite Soviet track and field throwers/sprinters/jumpers as the ceiling-
effect claims it responds to. Applying "keep it for maintenance, not for further gains" to
a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
different reasoning.
**Example** — A discus thrower whose squat numbers have plateaued relative to further
distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
than dropping squats from the program entirely.

a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —
the Chapter 1 idea (tie-in effect) this heuristic's "stimulational factor" speculation
echoes.

=================== claim--aerobic-anaerobic-energy-system-transfer-asymmetry.md
# Aerobic-to-Anaerobic-Alactate Transfer Is Broad and One-Directional; Anaerobic-Alactate-to-Aerobic Transfer Is Almost Absent
**What it is** — Tables 104-109 (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 149-154) report, for pairs
of energy-system training loads (aerobic, anaerobic-alactate, anaerobic-lactate), how many
of a set of physiological indices (heart rate, respiratory rate, lung ventilation, oxygen
reserve/debt, VO2max, blood lactate, energy expenditure/source, muscle fiber type, and
effect on time-to-sports-form) are "fully transferred," "frequently transferred," or
"non-transferred" from one training-load type to the other. The pattern is asymmetric, not
mutual, between each pair:
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: mostly transferable — Bondarchuk states "6 of 7" of
  the cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices are "fully transferable" (Table 104,
  PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable factors are specifically blood-lactate
  level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with different
  fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers in
  anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: broadly transferable both ways — "of the 16 tests
  looked at, only four were non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146); the
  anaerobic-lactate load actually *shortens* the time to enter sports form in aerobic
  training, while aerobic training does not shorten anaerobic-lactate's timeline (PDF pp.
  163-165, 171, printed pp. 146-148, 154).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: almost no transfer — "non-transferable factors here
  are all the remaining factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147),
  attributed to the oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus
  the oxygen-dependent structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: also limited, though the reverse direction
  (anaerobic-lactate loads shorten anaerobic-alactate's time to sports form, but not vice
  versa) shows a similar one-way asymmetry to the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate pair (Tables
  106-107, PDF pp. 164, 169, printed pp. 147, 152).
Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of the practical upshot of well-combined
aerobic/anaerobic training: "S. Auita" (almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held
world records simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within
tenths of a second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional
career bests: 200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11.
(PDF p. 172, printed p. 155.)
**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation is fiber-type recruitment: aerobic
training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers, while anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch) fibers, and he states plainly
for at least one asymmetry that "it is not known why" one direction shortens
time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed p. 147) — the author
himself flags this as an open question, not a resolved mechanism. Do not read a fuller
physiological explanation into this than the fiber-type note the text actually gives.
**When to apply** — Use this asymmetry as a caution against assuming energy-system
training transfers symmetrically: a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for
anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate capacity (per the "fully transferred" majority in
Tables 104-105), but a block of anaerobic-alactate (pure sprint/power) work should **not**
be expected to build aerobic capacity — per this data it does not, on all but 2 of 15
tracked physiological indices. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all
three energy systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target
the intended adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning
and energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`) — this
entry's asymmetry finding sharpens that general principle into a specific, one-directional
claim about which energy-system work can substitute for which.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported** for the aggregate Tables 104-109
findings (described as "collective data" in each table's own title, i.e. pooled across
Bondarchuk's tested athletes, sample size not stated in the excerpted pages).
**Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a single named-athlete case
offered as illustration, not independent evidence. The tested population is elite Soviet
and international middle/long-distance track athletes; the specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards. Applying this energy-system transfer asymmetry
directly to football conditioning (a repeated-sprint, intermittent-effort sport rather than
a continuous single-energy-system event) is Inference — no football or team-sport
population appears anywhere in this book.
**Example** — A program that substitutes heavy sprint/power ("anaerobic-alactate")
conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build aerobic capacity, is not
supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices showed no transfer in that
direction. The reverse substitution (using aerobic work to partially support
anaerobic-alactate capacity) has much more support in this data (Table 104).
**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer
asymmetry; cross-reference with `method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
for Eric's own energy-system programming framework, and with
[[claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]] for the companion finding
on how far training segment distances (rather than energy-system type) transfer within a
single distance-running event.

# The Longer the Competitive Distance, the Wider the Range of Segment Distances That Transfer to It — Except at the Ultra-Endurance Extreme
**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase
in the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments" — 800m
and 1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
steeplechase and women's 3000m start from 600m and 400m respectively; 5000m runners' range
starts around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women) — i.e., the
*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
longer. (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144.) Representative correlation values: men's
800m showed its strongest correlations with the 400m, 600m, and 1000m segments (0.700-0.912,
Table 89), with a sharp drop by the 1500m and further by 3000-5000m; women's 3000m showed
positive transfer across every tested segment, strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m
(0.725-0.906, Table 99). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners
(and 10km-walk women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer*
than the competitive distance, "because in sports practice similar tests do not exist" —
there is nothing longer to test against. (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)
**Why it works** — Bondarchuk attributes the general pattern to "the specifics of the
interaction of systems involved in the training effect" — different aerobic/anaerobic-
alactate/anaerobic-lactate energy-system demands at different distances (general systemic
reactions) plus the individual athlete's short- and long-term adaptational responses
(specific reactions). (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) He does not fully resolve *why* the
transfer range widens with distance beyond this general systems-interaction language.
**Inference:** one possible reading is that longer events draw on a broader mix of energy
systems and pacing demands, so a wider band of training distances can stress a
physiologically relevant system for that event; this interpretation is this entry's own
reading, not stated by the author, and no outside exercise-physiology source was checked
in this ingest to confirm it.
**When to apply** — Use as historical support for distance-specific training range
selection: shorter competitive events (800m-1500m) can be trained effectively with a
narrower, shorter set of segment distances; longer events (5000m-marathon) benefit from
(and require) a wider spread of training distances, from well below race distance up to
race distance itself, to cover the full transfer range this data shows. **Eric's
baseline:** HHPR 5355 already treats aerobic-system training for speed-power athletes as
mainly serving inter-effort recovery rather than distance capacity, kept below anaerobic
threshold at roughly a 1:1-1:2 work:rest ratio (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and
energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.51`) — this book's population is exclusively
dedicated distance-event specialists, a very different training context from a
speed-power athlete's incidental aerobic work, so this entry's distance-range findings
should not be imported into football conditioning design without that distinction in mind.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
middle/long/ultra-distance runners and race walkers, both sexes; the specific segment
distances and correlation values are dataset-specific. This entry covers **running/walking
segment distances only** — it says nothing about strength, jump, or throw-exercise
transfer to endurance events (not tested in this chapter). Applying "wider transfer range
for longer events" to a team-sport repeated-sprint or intermittent-endurance context
(football's actual endurance demand, per `method-baseline.md`'s energy-systems framing) is
Inference: football conditioning is not a single continuous-distance competitive event in
the way every sport in this dataset is.
**Example** — A 10,000m runner's program using training distances from 600m intervals up
to marathon-length long runs is well-supported by this data's transfer-range findings; a
marathoner's program should not expect any additional transfer benefit from segments
longer than the marathon itself, since no such segment exists to test or train.
**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — general classification
these segment distances fall under (specialized-developmental to competitive, depending on
how close the segment is to full race distance).

=================== claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns.md
# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier
**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). **High
jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
0.400 level" for running exercises specifically. Instead, per his prose (PDF p. 105,
printed p. 88), "the most informative and transferable exercise appears to be the vertical
jump with a short run-up," at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women) — **note an
unresolved source discrepancy**: those exact figures match the "10-fold jump from place"
row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965), not the row literally labeled
"Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women 0.680-0.808, which
the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may be a
translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's row
label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian or
a second translation. Barbell snatch showed almost no
transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)
**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested, but this
connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation. High
jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.
**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
long jumpers, high jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole vaulters, both sexes. The "high jump
breaks the pattern" finding is specific to Bondarchuk's Soviet-era high jump technique
population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
data exists in this source.
**Example** — A long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique jumps (at
reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
transfers the same way.
**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

46	sit" could borrow the *format* (competitive-result band -> matching assistance-exercise

49	**Related** — No existing library entry covers normative benchmark tables directly; see
