54	# Specialized-Developmental Runs (Flying 30m, Blocks 30-200m) Correlate Strongly with Sprint/Hurdle Competitive Results
55	**What it is** — Tables 41-50 (PDF pp. 78-87, printed pp. 61-70) report correlation
56	coefficients between competitive results and other specialized-developmental/competitive
57	run distances, for men's and women's 100m, 200m, 400m, 110m/400m hurdles (men) and
58	100m/400m hurdles (women), each split by "high level" vs. "low level" athlete
59	qualification (the table note: high-level in the numerator, low-level in the denominator
60	for these specific tables — Tables 41-50 only; see the reversed convention noted in
61	`_book.md` for the throws tables). Bondarchuk's own summary: "the coefficients of
62	correlation in most cases are in the range of 0.700-0.800" (PDF p. 87, printed p. 70).
63	Representative individual values pulled directly (high-qualification/low-qualification):
64	100m runners' 30m-flying-start correlated 0.678/0.778 with the 30m-from-blocks segment and
65	0.756/0.876 with the 100m-from-blocks segment (Table 41); 110m hurdlers' 110m-hurdles
66	result correlated only 0.562/0.420 with the 200m-from-blocks segment, the weakest pairing
67	in that table (Table 44); 400m hurdlers' 400m-hurdles result correlated as high as
68	0.890/0.806 with the 600m-from-a-high-start segment (Table 45).
69	**Why it works** — The tables report the correlations without explaining them. **Inference:**
70	reading this through
71	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and
72	[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — these are all specialized-developmental
73	or competitive-class exercises (shorter/longer runs at or near race intensity), sharing
74	most of the sprint or hurdle event's biomechanics and energy-system demands, which would
75	predict the high correlation observed — but this connection is this entry's own reading,
76	not a claim the author makes for this specific table set.
77	**When to apply** — Use as historical evidence that assistance runs at varied distances
78	(flying starts, sub-maximal and supra-maximal segment lengths) are a reliably transferable
79	training tool for sprint/hurdle athletes, supporting programs that use varied-distance
80	sprint work rather than only full-distance reps. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355's
81	linear-sprint testing already uses split-time interpretation by physical quality (0-10m
82	acceleration, 30-40m speed) rather than total time alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed
83	and sprint," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`) — this book's high
84	segment-to-total correlations support treating those splits as meaningfully diagnostic,
85	not just a total-time proxy.
86	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
87	Soviet-era male and female sprinters and hurdlers (refs implicit in the tables' athlete
88	qualification split; exact sample sizes are not given in the excerpted pages). The
89	correlations described are all between running-based specialized-developmental/
90	competitive exercises — this entry does NOT cover strength or jump-exercise transfer,
91	which is markedly weaker (see
92	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
93	[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]]). Applying these specific
94	coefficients to football skill-position speed training is Inference: football speed
95	development sits inside a team-sport context with far less training-time devoted purely
96	to sprinting than a specialized Soviet track program, so the magnitude of these
97	correlations should not be assumed to hold as-is.
98	**Example** — A 200m runner's training program built heavily around 150m and 300m
99	repeats at race-adjacent intensity is well-supported by this data (150m-to-200m and
100	300m-to-200m correlations were among the higher entries in Table 42), more so than a
101	program relying mainly on much shorter (30m) segments for that specific event.
102	**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
103	correlated exercises fall into. [[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] —
104	the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
105	group.
106	confidence: supported
107	=================== claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance.md
108	# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts
109	**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
110	against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
111	vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
112	forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
113	**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
114	preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
115	but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
116	appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
117	cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
118	range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
119	p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and triple
120	jump from place each showed positive transfer only on two-to-three of five levels for most
121	events, and high jump/pole vault-style single jumps were even more level-restricted for
122	sprint events specifically (not their own competitive event). He generalizes: "with an
123	increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises, there
124	is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
125	exercises over long ground-contact segments (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
126	jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.)
127	**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
128	the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
129	"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
130	and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
131	acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) **Inference:** reading
132	this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real
133	sprint-relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing
134	jump does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict
135	exactly
136	the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.
137	**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
138	sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
139	over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
140	velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
141	consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
142	diagnostic/training value.
143	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
144	sprinters and hurdlers, both sexes; "leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from
145	place" are specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding
146	or plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
147	levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
148	conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
149	single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference; no outside
150	plyometrics source was checked in this ingest to confirm the pattern holds beyond
151	Bondarchuk's own track and field dataset.
152	**Example** — A sprint-development block choosing between a session of standing long
153	jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m would, per this
154	data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider range of athlete
155	ability levels.
156	**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the
157	running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.
158	[[claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns]] — the parallel (and partly consistent)
159	finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.
160	confidence: supported
161	=================== claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling.md
162	# The Barbell Snatch and Half Squat Transfer to Sprinting Only Up to a Narrow, Specific Performance Band, Then Stop
163	**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell
164	snatch and half squat (with barbell on shoulders) against 100m/200m/400m and hurdle
165	results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
166	interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
167	confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.
168	Examples with locators: men's 100m snatch/squat "cumulative effect" only up to
169	11.10-11.40s (Table 51: snatch coefficients range from -0.186 at 10.20-10.50s up to only
170	0.396 at 11.10-11.40s); women's snatch shows an effect on only one band, 12.70-12.79s
171	(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,
172	with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55 itself at PDF p. 95,
173	printed p. 78; the "not seen" summary sentence and the 0.196-0.320 range are Bondarchuk's
174	own text at PDF p. 89, printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
175	were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
176	(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)
177	**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: "the cumulative effect from strength
178	exercises will appear only when they are close to the competitive event according to the
179	biomechanical aspects and methodological parameters" (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85).
180	**Inference:** in the terms this book itself defines, the snatch and squat are
181	specialized-preparatory exercises (per [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]),
182	sharing muscle groups with sprinting but not its movement structure, velocity, or
183	ground-contact regime — placing them, per
184	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], further from the competitive event
185	in the transfer chain than the running-based exercises in
186	[[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]]; this specific
187	classification-based reading of "close... according to the biomechanical aspects" is this
188	entry's own, not spelled out by the author in this passage. He explicitly declines to
189	call this "ineffectiveness," instead suggesting the missing transfer could be a
190	methodological artifact (rep count, session compactness, intensity zones used) rather than
191	a fixed property of the exercises. (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85.)
192	**When to apply** — Use as historical caution against assuming barbell strength numbers
193	(snatch, squat) will keep predicting sprint improvement once an athlete passes a certain
194	performance level; per this data, once an athlete is already fast, further improvement in
195	these lifts stops tracking with further sprint improvement. This does not mean drop the
196	lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for
197	Bondarchuk's own prescription on that point) — it means stop expecting them to be the
198	driver of further sprint gains at that point.
199	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
200	Soviet-era sprinters/hurdlers, both sexes, tested with a specific barbell snatch and a
201	half-squat-with-barbell-on-shoulders (not a full back squat, front squat, or trap-bar
202	variant); the finding should not be assumed to hold for a different strength exercise
203	variation without its own data. This is track and field data; extending "barbell strength
204	work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed past a certain level" to football speed
205	training is Inference. No outside source was checked in this ingest to confirm whether
206	this pattern holds beyond Bondarchuk's own dataset; treat it as this book's finding only
207	until cross-checked.
208	**Example** — A high-level 100m sprinter already running 10.2-10.4s should not expect
209	squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this data; a
210	developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the band
211	where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.
212	**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the much
213	stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.
214	[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — Bondarchuk's own
215	prescription for what to do once an exercise stops producing further transfer.
216	confidence: supported
217	=================== claim--three-types-of-training-transfer.md
218	# Training Transfer Comes in Four Flavors: Positive, Negative, Neutral, and Indifferent
219	**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three standard types of training transfer plus a fourth
220	he flags as rarer and specific to high-level athletes (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15):
221	- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
222	- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
223	  another.
224	- **Neutral** (also "indifferent" in some literature he cites): no measurable effect
225	  either way.
226	- **Indifferent/double effect** (his own added category, "met more rarely," specifically
227	  in high-level athletes using a complex of different exercises): one exercise can help
228	  and hurt at the same time along different dimensions, e.g. heavier-implement throws
229	  positive for strength but negative for technique — "there is a noticeable worsening of
230	  technique in some throws with the use of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]). Bondarchuk
231	  gives a specific example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/anaerobic running in
232	  general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory function but worsened
233	  walking technique (ref [94]), a case of positive-physiological/negative-technical
234	  double effect. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)
235	**Why it works** — Bondarchuk gives no mechanism for why transfer takes these particular
236	forms; he presents the three-way split as received terminology ("in the specialized
237	literature it is also possible to find 'indifferent' transfer," without naming a specific
238	source for that term) and adds the fourth (double-effect) category as his own observation.
239	**Note on scope:** Chapter 1's earlier discussion of E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical
240	elements" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3; see
241	[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]) is presented by Bondarchuk as the
242	basis for the *specifist* position on transfer generally, not explicitly linked by him to
243	this positive/negative/neutral/indifferent typology — this entry does not claim that link
244	was Bondarchuk's own. **Inference:** the double-effect category is a plausible, useful name
245	for a pattern coaches encounter often (an exercise that builds one quality while degrading
246	another), but this is this entry's own framing, not a claim from the text about how common
247	or well-recognized that pattern is elsewhere.
248	**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new
249	exercise: is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect**
250	where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
251	technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
252	illustration — flag any high-volume general-conditioning block for a technical,
253	timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect risk, not
254	just a "general conditioning is fine" default.
255	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The category examples given (heavier
256	implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
257	technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
258	reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
259	Population is elite track and field throwers and race walkers; extending "double effect"
260	reasoning to football (e.g., heavy sled work degrading sprint mechanics) is Inference,
261	plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.
262	**Example** — **Inference:** a college lineman doing high-volume heavy sled pushes for
263	GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
264	effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
265	reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
266	example here.
267	**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
268	staging) — the mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases plausibly run through
269	(mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions).
270	confidence: supported
271	=================== claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal.md
272	# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery
273	**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
274	throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
275	0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
276	women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary: "there is
277	almost always a place for mutually correlated interrelationships... the amounts of these
278	interrelationships are sufficiently great," with only two exceptions found in the entire
279	dataset (javelin: no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and the 3-4kg standing
280	throw; no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements). (PDF p. 132, printed p.
281	115.) He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
282	(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
283	Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
284	implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
285	dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
286	his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (Tables 85-86, PDF pp. 130-131,
287	printed pp. 113-114). Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his
288	implement-weight throws increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances
289	(Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).
290	**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
291	"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
292	and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
293	muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
294	**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
295	close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
296	movement, only the resistance changes), which under
297	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
298	positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
299	stated by the author in these terms.
300	**When to apply** — This is the strongest, most consistent transfer finding in the entire
301	book: for throwing events specifically, varying implement weight while keeping the
302	competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training method across nearly the
303	full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any strength, jump, or sprint
304	assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter. He does flag a real caveat: heavier
305	implements can degrade technique (release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect
306	he says clears up "in several weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the
307	double-effect pattern named in [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].
308	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
309	finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa/Shulta individual case data (Tables
310	85-88) is **untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not
311	as independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
312	rather than proof. Population throughout is elite Soviet-bloc throwers (Olympic and world
313	champions/record holders for the case studies). This finding is specific to implements
314	that can be made lighter or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact
315	(shot, discus, javelin, hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight
316	manipulation in most football skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement
317	identical" as a general training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a
318	quarterback) is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.
319	**Example** — A hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of 5-6 different
320	implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight) targeting both speed and
321	strength qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as
322	a transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
323	that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).
324	**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
325	explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
326	— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
327	group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
328	heavier-implement technique caveat.
329	confidence: supported
330	=================== claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect.md
331	# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau
332	**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
333	four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
334	bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
335	transfer to the competitive throw, but **only up to a specific result level for each
336	exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive improvement
337	disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m
338	(men) / 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended
339	furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
340	65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three.
341	In shot put, snatch ended at 17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m
342	(men)/14-25m (women, likely an OCR artifact for a narrower band), squat at 19-20m
343	(men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). In javelin, snatch and power
344	clean both ended at 65-70m (men); at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for
345	either the squat or the bench press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
346	50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat "showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135,
347	printed pp. 116-118.) Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the
348	close of this chapter: "specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an
349	increase in the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports
350	mastery. Further on, they do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.)
351	**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
352	levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
353	common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
354	strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
355	level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
356	technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
357	exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
358	binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
359	himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.
360	**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
361	athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
362	specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
363	athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
364	their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
365	competitive improvement.
366	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
367	throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
368	clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
369	depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
370	1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
371	"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
372	[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
373	explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
374	maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
375	athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
376	here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
377	throw.
378	**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
379	level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
380	distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
381	technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
382	strength work maintained rather than chased.
383	**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
384	specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.
385	[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — what to do with
386	strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.
387	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the parallel (and even more limited)
388	ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.
389	confidence: supported

=================== claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification.md
# Bondarchuk Publishes 34 Normative Tables Linking Assistance-Exercise Results to Competitive-Result Bands, by Age and Qualification
**What it is** — Tables 1-34 (PDF pp. 44-67, printed pp. 27-50; this ingest sampled
representative tables rather than transcribing all 34) give normative "model
characteristics": for a given competitive-result band (e.g., 100m in 10.00-10.20s vs.

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts
**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and triple
jump from place each showed positive transfer only on two-to-three of five levels for most
events, and high jump/pole vault-style single jumps were even more level-restricted for
sprint events specifically (not their own competitive event). He generalizes: "with an
increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises, there
is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
exercises over long ground-contact segments (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.)
**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) **Inference:** reading
this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real
sprint-relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing
jump does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict
exactly
the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.
**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
diagnostic/training value.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
sprinters and hurdlers, both sexes; "leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from
place" are specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding
or plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference; no outside
plyometrics source was checked in this ingest to confirm the pattern holds beyond
Bondarchuk's own track and field dataset.
**Example** — A sprint-development block choosing between a session of standing long
jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m would, per this
data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider range of athlete
ability levels.

running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.

finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.

**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell

results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.

(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,

printed p. 78; the "not seen" summary sentence and the 0.196-0.320 range are Bondarchuk's

were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands

specialized-preparatory exercises (per [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]),

ground-contact regime — placing them, per
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], further from the competitive event

[[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]]; this specific
classification-based reading of "close... according to the biomechanical aspects" is this

call this "ineffectiveness," instead suggesting the missing transfer could be a
methodological artifact (rep count, session compactness, intensity zones used) rather than

=================== claim--three-types-of-training-transfer.md
# Training Transfer Comes in Four Flavors: Positive, Negative, Neutral, and Indifferent
**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three standard types of training transfer plus a fourth
he flags as rarer and specific to high-level athletes (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15):
- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
  another.
- **Neutral** (also "indifferent" in some literature he cites): no measurable effect
  either way.
- **Indifferent/double effect** (his own added category, "met more rarely," specifically
  in high-level athletes using a complex of different exercises): one exercise can help
  and hurt at the same time along different dimensions, e.g. heavier-implement throws
  positive for strength but negative for technique — "there is a noticeable worsening of
  technique in some throws with the use of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]). Bondarchuk
  gives a specific example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/anaerobic running in
  general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory function but worsened
  walking technique (ref [94]), a case of positive-physiological/negative-technical
  double effect. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)
**Why it works** — Bondarchuk gives no mechanism for why transfer takes these particular
forms; he presents the three-way split as received terminology ("in the specialized
literature it is also possible to find 'indifferent' transfer," without naming a specific
source for that term) and adds the fourth (double-effect) category as his own observation.
**Note on scope:** Chapter 1's earlier discussion of E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical
elements" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3; see
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]) is presented by Bondarchuk as the
basis for the *specifist* position on transfer generally, not explicitly linked by him to
this positive/negative/neutral/indifferent typology — this entry does not claim that link
was Bondarchuk's own. **Inference:** the double-effect category is a plausible, useful name
for a pattern coaches encounter often (an exercise that builds one quality while degrading
another), but this is this entry's own framing, not a claim from the text about how common
or well-recognized that pattern is elsewhere.
**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new
exercise: is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect**
where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
illustration — flag any high-volume general-conditioning block for a technical,
timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect risk, not
just a "general conditioning is fine" default.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The category examples given (heavier
implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
Population is elite track and field throwers and race walkers; extending "double effect"
reasoning to football (e.g., heavy sled work degrading sprint mechanics) is Inference,
plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.
**Example** — **Inference:** a college lineman doing high-volume heavy sled pushes for
GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
example here.
**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — the mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases plausibly run through
(mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions).
confidence: supported

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery
**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary: "there is
almost always a place for mutually correlated interrelationships... the amounts of these
interrelationships are sufficiently great," with only two exceptions found in the entire
dataset (javelin: no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and the 3-4kg standing
throw; no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements). (PDF p. 132, printed p.
115.) He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (Tables 85-86, PDF pp. 130-131,
printed pp. 113-114). Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his
implement-weight throws increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances
(Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).
**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.
**When to apply** — This is the strongest, most consistent transfer finding in the entire
book: for throwing events specifically, varying implement weight while keeping the
competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training method across nearly the
full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any strength, jump, or sprint
assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter. He does flag a real caveat: heavier
implements can degrade technique (release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect
he says clears up "in several weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the
double-effect pattern named in [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa/Shulta individual case data (Tables
85-88) is **untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not
as independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. Population throughout is elite Soviet-bloc throwers (Olympic and world
champions/record holders for the case studies). This finding is specific to implements
that can be made lighter or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact
(shot, discus, javelin, hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight
manipulation in most football skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement
identical" as a general training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a
quarterback) is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.
**Example** — A hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of 5-6 different
implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight) targeting both speed and
strength qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as
a transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).
**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat.

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau
**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw, but **only up to a specific result level for each
exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive improvement
disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m
(men) / 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended
furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three.
In shot put, snatch ended at 17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m
(men)/14-25m (women, likely an OCR artifact for a narrower band), squat at 19-20m
(men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). In javelin, snatch and power
clean both ended at 65-70m (men); at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for
either the squat or the bench press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat "showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135,
printed pp. 116-118.) Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the
close of this chapter: "specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an
increase in the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports
mastery. Further on, they do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.)
**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.
**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.
**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.
**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
strength work maintained rather than chased.
**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.

strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.

content.content:
##### PDF page 18 (viewer 19) #####
Chapter 1

A Brief Overview of Training
Transfer

The transfer of training is one of the central problems in the theory and practice of
physical education.  The reason for this is that it is in the transfer of training that the
learning and improvement of technique and likewise the development of the related, or
other physical qualities (abilities) take place.  However, we also come up against the
interactions of the training means used at this time.  This has a place even when using
ordinary training sessions with only one exercise.  The exercise can leave traces, as for
example, after executing the first training session in a specific manner, it has an influence
on execution of the second (next) session.  Dynamic changes take place in all systems of
the body in order to ensure the sports activity.  This shows up mainly on the functioning
of the central nervous and heart-circulatory systems.

Even in the first decades of the 20th century, specialists in many scientific areas (classical
and sports physiology, classical and sports psychology, neurophysiology, biomechanics,
theory and methods of physical education, and others) began to carry out experiments to
determine situations in which the acquisition of an earlier learned skill in one exercise
had a positive influence on the learning of another exercise later on.  Or, in cases where
an increase in the level of sports results, as for example in exercise A, makes it possible
to improve results in exercise B.

1


##### PDF page 19 (viewer 20) #####
In further studies, it was shown that the transfer of training not only can be positive, but
negative.  In many cases, as for example an increase in strength capabilities in exercise A,
there is no positive or negative affect on exercise B.

In the theory and methods of physical education, the process of training transfer is
subdivided into the transfer of skills and the transfer of physical abilities.  Each of these
problems is looked at separately.  In this chapter, the essence of the three basic theories of
transfer are looked at.  Those siding with the first of these we conditionally call
“specifists”, second, “generalists” and third, “holistics”.

2


##### PDF page 20 (viewer 21) #####
The Specifists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training
Transfer

One of those who established the base for specificity was E. L. Torndyke [223].  She
called it the theory of identical elements.  In agreement with her, the transfer of training is
seen when in two types of activities, there is some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of
elements. Their absence does not make it possible to have transfer.  This appearance is
completely specific according to its essence.

The transfer of training takes place by using earlier acquired associated ties [284, 287,
288, 294, 304].  Between them there must be identical elements in a definite order.  The
theory of identical elements was criticized by many native specialists in the area of
classical and sports physiology and psychology.  They quoted the learning’s of I. P.
Pavlov and believed that naturally formed conditioned reflexes lie in the activity of the
central nervous system.  They do not negate the significance of old associations in the
systemic activity of the higher segments of the brain.

The influence of the coinciding “working” elements in the process of forming functional
systems was noted by P.K. Anokhin [7].  According to him, the functional systems are
only as great as displayed in the existing exercise.  In execution of most exercises, similar
muscle groups participate.  Besides this, any activity ensures the functioning of one or
another body system in the process of adaptation that takes place in response to the
external or internal effect.

Similar muscular groups appear to work in the formation of simple as well as complex,
physical exercises (according to their coordinational make-up) [25, 26, 79].  This allowed
several authors to speak of the multi-sided structure of physical exercises [50, 128, 143].

Physical exercises possess multi-functional and multi-system properties.  The multi-
functionality ensures activation of similar organs and body systems [94, 126, 140, 267].
3


##### PDF page 21 (viewer 22) #####
As a result, this produces definite adaptational changes which serve to increase the level
of their functionality.  These changes can then also be seen in execution of other
exercises.

Multi-system actions appear in the formation of complex coordinational movements. The
latter can be composed of definite “selections” of simple local movements, each of which
is used in many track and field events.  For example, active extension and flexion of the
legs occurs in many sprint events, in the hurdles, jumps and throws.  Local movements
can be improved outside the structure of some complex coordinational exercise, and later
used as a “building block” for learning movements having multi-links [265].

4


##### PDF page 22 (viewer 23) #####
The Generalists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training
Transfer

 The viewpoints of the generalists are distinguished from the specifists according to their
formulation of training transfer.  Generalists recommend several general and specialized
pedagogical principles which give special attention to harmonious, all-round
development of the athletes in the process of sports improvement.  The essence of this
viewpoint is in the principle of unity of general and specialized preparation. Separately,
each cannot resolve the problems presented before it.  General preparation creates the
prerequisites for increasing sports achievements in the specialized area.  Note that all-
round development of the athlete is determined by the laws of formation and
improvement of motor skills.  The basic idea of general preparation somehow appears to
be realized in the process of sports improvement with a transfer of training from the
general to the specialized preparation [18, 153, 212].

In the theory and methods of physical education, it is recommended that coaches use the
unity of general and specialized preparation when constructing the multi-year process of
sports improvement, as well as during separate cycles (periods) of sports form
development.  Thus, on the base stage of preparation, which lasts from four to six years,
it is believed that with the use of general preparation, it is possible to lay down a full
value foundation for future movements, ensure all-round harmonious development of the
body, increase the general level of the body’s functional capabilities, create a rich fund of
differently formed movement skills and abilities, and form beginning basic sports
mastery [154].  They believe that the achievement of sports results on a given stage does
not influence the next stage or objective.  This is realized later on the stage of maximum
realization of sports capabilities.

Generalists recommend that cycles of sports form development be broken up into general
and specialized preparatory stages, where naturally, a base is created at the beginning
with the use of a large number of general preparation means and later, on the stage of
5

specialized preparation, realization of them.  This idea is maintained and used in different

increase takes place in another exercise.

In negative transfer of training there is always a negative interaction between the
exercises being used.  Here, with increased preparation in one exercise, there is a
simultaneous decrease in other exercises.

training does not show any affect on another training.

indifferent transfer.  This is especially so when training high level athletes who use a

the body in order to ensure the sports activity.  This shows up mainly on the functioning
of the central nervous and heart-circulatory systems.

and sports physiology, classical and sports psychology, neurophysiology, biomechanics,
theory and methods of physical education, and others) began to carry out experiments to
determine situations in which the acquisition of an earlier learned skill in one exercise

It is completely natural that active “close” and “far” areas, which appear as a
consequence of a generalized distribution or spread of the excitatory-inhibitory impulses,
appear in a definite form to improve the functional ability of a body system due to non-
specific adaptational changes.

Knowing the regularity of the “breaks” in activeness in the working nerve centers on the
non-working areas can explain many questions about the transfer of training in the speed-
strength events in track and field and other sports.  Their expression will be accompanied
10


##### PDF page 28 (viewer 29) #####
with great changes in the understanding of the principles not only of training transfer, but
the very method of training.  All of this is in the future.

Now, we should take note of a major deficiency in the theory of the holistics in that they
indirectly call for the use of one method of training for increasing the functional
capabilities of the blood vessels, cardio-vascular and respiratory systems, in order to get
corresponding adaptational changes in the neuro-muscular system.  This leads to
disharmony, as the athlete enters the highest training state in non-specific exercises at the
start and only after this, after several weeks, enters a state of sports form in the specific
exercises.  It would be possible to ignore this if the functional levels achieved in non-
specific exercises were maintained while the athlete was still achieving corresponding
increases in his physical preparation in the specific training means.  However, the level of
trainedness decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized
exercises.

In the track and field jumps and throws and likewise in the hurdles, there is agreement
with the holistics that is necessary to first develop the physical capabilities and only after
this, perfect technical mastery.  Thus the “block” method of constructing cycles of sports
form development oversees the separate preparatory periods in the blocks of physical and
technical preparation [49].  Those in agreement with this concept do not believe that
simultaneously introducing means of technical preparation into the training process
develops the physical abilities together with improvement of technique.

In these instances, there is a theoretical and practical error working at the base of the
artificial division of form and content since they are united in all of their displays.  In the
theory and methods of physical education this unity is expressed in the principle of
conjugated training effects.  This was proposed in the 1960’s by head coach and scientist
V.M. Dyachkov [81]. The essence of this method will be looked at further on since it
provides answers to many questions that require a straight forward understanding of the
training transfer process.

11


##### PDF page 29 (viewer 30) #####
The Principle of Conjugated Training Effects

The use of training means for developing physical abilities and improving technical
mastery is in accord with this principle.  These two factors should coincide and
correspond to the competitive exercise according to their basic characteristics.  Later on,
this principle was modified by other specialists who called it dynamic correspondence
and the principle of resolving motor actions.  [157]. According to U.V. Menkhin [157]
the conjugate principle should affect not only the competitive event, but all the
specialized activity as a whole.

Using the sport of gymnastics as an example, Menkhin showed that the best form of
conjugation appears when the physical preparation ensures five main components of
preparation for technical improvement or for learning technique:
• Development of the motor qualities that are necessary for a specific activity that is
sufficiently localized in the muscle groups;
• A high level of motor qualities that define the demands of the biodynamic
structure of gymnastic elements;
• Suitability for realizing the motor potential in the most common forms of motor
activity, that characterize the potential physical preparation needed for mastering
technique;
• Suitability for fulfilling long duration work in specific events in all-round
competition that guarantees the gymnasts motor activity reliability [repeat
ability];
• Suitability for realizing the motor potential in competitive combinations [routines]
which is the main objective of the gymnast.

We will not purposely end on the main components proposed by U.V. Menkhin in
gymnastics as we believe that it can be used in the technical disciplines of track and field.

12


##### PDF page 30 (viewer 31) #####
The conjugate principle of training effects was used by us in working out the principle of
all-round specialized preparation [265]. Over many years, it envisioned sports
improvement through the use of primarily specialized preparation means.  General
preparation means were used to a lesser extent and only for general warm ups and during
the time of using restorative measures. Special-preparatory and special-developmental
exercises create the “base”, “the foundation”, for improving sports results in a
competitive event on each level in the cycle of developing sports form that produced the
greatest sports improvement.

The number of special-preparatory and special-developmental exercises used in each
consecutive cycle (period) of developing sports form depends on the tasks to be
accomplished.  They should be sufficient for resolution of the tasks.  Here, the transfer
effect depends not only on the number of special-preparatory and special-developmental
exercises used, but on their “newness” and the strength of their effect which should be
greater in each consecutive cycle of sports form development.  This makes it possible to
achieve a new level of adaptation, which serves to increase the sports result and naturally,
the transfer of training.
13


##### PDF page 31 (viewer 32) #####
Types of Training Transfer

There are three types of training transfer: positive, negative, and neutral.  In the
specialized literature it is also possible to find “indifferent” transfer.

Positive transfer of training means that there is a positive effect of one exercise on
another.  In other words, with an increase in the sports result in one exercise, a parallel
increase takes place in another exercise.

In negative transfer of training there is always a negative interaction between the
exercises being used.  Here, with increased preparation in one exercise, there is a
simultaneous decrease in other exercises.

In neutral transfer of training there is no increase or decrease in sports achievement.  The
training does not show any affect on another training.

In addition to these three noted forms of training transfer we more rarely meet with
indifferent transfer.  This is especially so when training high level athletes who use a
whole complex of different exercises, and depends on their coordination structure and
strength of their influence.  At the present time, the interrelationships between the
exercises are complex and unpredictable, and they may have a double effect on one
another. For example, there may be a positive affect on increasing the functional
capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the technique an exercise [92].
In track and field, there is a noticeable worsening of technique in some throws with the
use of heavier implements [18, 152]. In these cases, with an increase in strength, there is
a negative change in the process of executing separate elements as well the entire
movement as a whole [152].

The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent transfer) is most frequently
explained by the use of exercises which, from the beginning, interfere with the unity
between form and content.  Examples of indifferent transfer can be in the systems of
14


##### PDF page 32 (viewer 33) #####
training as for example, by athletes specializing in different walking events.  Included
here is the use of a high volume of aerobic and anaerobic running for long periods of
time, as in the general preparatory stage.  In this training there is a noted improvement in
the functional abilities of the heart-circulatory, respiratory and blood vessel systems and a
worsening of walking technique [94].

There are similar inter-effects that come up in other sports.  In walking it is possible to
get away from the negative influence by using mainly specialized-developmental and
competitive exercises.  In certain running events, hurdles and throws, it is possible to
maneuver between “good” and “poor” in selecting exercises, so that there would be more
good ones rather than poor ones.  This makes it possible to eliminate the negative
influence on technique in several weekly cycles.

15


##### PDF page 33 (viewer 34) #####
Transfer Factors

The theory of training transfer oversees the study of many carry-over factors, beginning
with the interaction between separate exercises and physical abilities to their mutual
influence in simple or complex movements.  We will address some of these basic carry-
over factors.  Foremost is the transfer of physical abilities and motor skills when using
different, according to form and content, means of training.  First is the influence of
general developmental exercises on specialized-preparatory, specialized-developmental,
or competitive exercises.  Second, is the effect of specialized-preparatory exercises on
specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.  Third are training questions on the
effect of specialized-developmental exercises on the competitive event.

Thus it is necessary to know how the general-preparatory, specialized-preparatory and
specialized-developmental exercises have an effect on the competitive exercise and
which form of the latter exercises has an influence on the general-preparatory,
specialized-preparatory and specialized-developmental exercises.

The transfer of training, within the limits of one exercise, is basically the same when
using simple or complex (according to their coordinational structure) exercises.  For
example, training the leg extensor muscles at one joint angle has a positive effect on
strength in other joint angles [95].  We come up with similar effects in the process of
using the bench press, the angle of the body and others.  In the training of throwers, when
using the entire throw, we simultaneously get an increase in sports results when throwing
from place.  In training long jumpers, when using jumps with a full or short run up, there
is a positive effect on the development of speed in the 30 or 60 meter run.

Throwing, as for example the standard weight in any track and field throw event, can
have a positive or negative influence on results when throwing a lighter or heavier weight
(implement).

16


##### PDF page 34 (viewer 35) #####
Transfer of training is also realized within the confines of whole motor actions.  The
specific system of training, as for example, with 800 meter runners, has an effect on
results in the 400 and 1500 meter runs.

In the theory and methods of physical education, there are many studies devoted to
learning about the influence of single physical capabilities (strength, speed, endurance),
acquired in certain motor actions on other actions [40, 91, 92, 94, 124]. Looked at were
the inter-influences of differently composed identical or other physical abilities.  Thus in
development of strength, what kinds of physical exercises and muscle work regimes
serve to develop absolute strength, speed-strength, or explosive muscle properties and
likewise strength endurance.  In the track and field sprints, in studying speed
development, specialists are interested in the influence of these or other means of training
for developing simple and complex motor reactions, speed and special endurance.

In studying endurance, the mutual relationship not only between specific physical
qualities such as general and speed endurance are looked at, but also factors such as the
energy that ensures work, functional power, functional economy (maximum utilization of
oxygen--max O2 uptake--during the time of work, the time limits possible when working
at maximum oxygen uptake, anaerobic threshold--AT, concentration of lactic acid and
oxygen debt).

17

-**What it is** — A four-stage shared map Weber uses to describe where an athlete sits in a program, so staff across strength and conditioning, rehab, and sports science can communicate quickly without re-litigating vocabulary. The stages: **Control** (single-joint, isolated activation, used early in rehab or with an athlete who cannot yet sequence joints), **Movement** (multi-joint, integrated patterns that are "viable and repeatable... without falling apart"), **Capacity** (building the "engine": volume and tolerance for work, where "a lot of athletes live for large parts of the year"), and **Maximum** (short exposures to peak speed, force, or power once capacity is built) (Lab 1A transcript, 00:06:05–00:08:32). Athletes move forward when ready and back to an earlier stage when needed.
